paragraphs.text: A rolled [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) from 1980, grown on the island whose tea plants and craft first came over from Fujian. Its label gives only [Taiwan](taiwan:on-a-label). That places the leaf on the island and says nothing of the mountain, township or cultivar it came from.

At forty-six years it belongs to the island's tradition of [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea. An oolong chosen for keeping starts well roasted and dry. It is roasted again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in, and it is kept cool, dark and sealed in between, while the liquor deepens over the years from amber towards red-brown. No standard says how many years make an oolong old. Those who give a figure put it somewhere between ten and thirty, and this tea is past both.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
